 Powered by Quartr Oct 28, 2026, 4:00 AM EDT Earnings calls summary
 Powered by Yahoo Scout UBS delivered robust Q3 2026 results with reported net profit of $2.7B, EPS of $0.85, and underlying pre-tax profit up 14% YoY to $4.1B. Integration of Credit Suisse is nearly complete, cost-income ratio improved to 68.7%, and management reaffirmed confidence in achieving a ~14% CET1 ratio and <70% cost/income target by year-end, despite macro and regulatory headwinds.
 Speaker 0 0:00:00 
 Ladies and gentlemen, good morning. Welcome to the UBS third quarter 2026 results. The conference must not be recorded for publication or broadcast. Analysts can register for questions at any time by pressing star and one on the telephone. Media representatives are invited to join this call in listen-only mode. Should you need operator assistance, please press star and zero. At this time, it is my pleasure to hand over to Sarah Mackey, UBS Investor Relations. Please go ahead, madam. 
 Speaker 1 0:00:35 
 Good morning and welcome, everyone. Before we start, I would like to draw your attention to our cautionary statement slide at the back of today's results presentation. Please also refer to the risk factors included in our annual report, together with additional disclosures in our SEC filings. Throughout our remarks, we will refer to underlying results in USD and make year-over-year comparisons unless stated otherwise. On slide 2, you can see our agenda for today. It is now my pleasure to hand over to Sergio Ermotti, Group CEO. 
 Speaker 2 0:01:10 
 Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. In an increasingly complex market environment, our strong third quarter performance once again demonstrated the benefits of our diversified global business model and disciplined execution. We remain focused on what we could control, deepening client relationships, prudently managing resources and risks, and finalizing the integration of Credit Suisse while delivering on our related financial ambitions. With a year-to-date return on CET1 capital of 17%, we are increasingly confident in our ability to outperform our 2026 exit rate return target. We remain on track to achieve our exit rate cost-income ratio target of less than 70%. Our global diversification remains a key source of strength and momentum. In APAC, our One Bank approach is driving year-to-date pre-tax profit margins towards 50%. In the U.S., our strategic investments continue to translate into consistently higher levels of profitability and growth. 
 Speaker 2 0:02:33 
 In Switzerland, the value clients place in our local and global capabilities is increasingly evident in our results, and we granted or renewed around CHF 40 billion of loans to businesses and households. Meanwhile, in EMEA, our enhanced scale is translating into stronger operating leverage in the region. More broadly, the breadth and depth of our offering allowed us to attract CHF 55 billion of inflows in Global Wealth Management. We also saw record demand for our Unified Global Alternatives strategies, further bolstering our scale and growth momentum. In the Investment Bank, we improved on our already best-in-class efficiency with record third-quarter performance reflecting the strength of our equities franchise and our ability to capture high return opportunities, particularly in Asia. As we enter the fourth quarter, investor sentiments remain measured amid elevated macroeconomic volatility, ongoing geopolitical tensions, and political uncertainty with consequential elections, including in the U.S. 
 Speaker 2 0:03:59 
 Against this backdrop, we are staying close to clients to help them navigate market conditions and capture opportunities. Our profitability and balance sheet for all seasons gives us the capacity to do this while also delivering on our capital return plans. We have repurchased $4.8 billion of shares and accrued $2.8 billion for our dividend year to date. We have already achieved the ambition we set early in the integration journey for 2026, with total capital returns now to exceed pre-acquisition levels. Over the next three months, we intend to repurchase $1.2 billion of shares, completing our current program. As usual, we will outline our capital return plans for 2027 with our fourth quarter results. Turning to the integration of Credit Suisse, we are in the last mile, and the finish line is in sight. 
 Speaker 2 0:05:12 
 Nearly all legacy applications are no longer in use, with 90% fully decommissioned, and as said, we are close to achieving our related financial ambitions. Of all we have accomplished over the last three years, I remain very proud of how our people come together under a common culture and vision. Our recent employee survey results continue to exceed financial services benchmarks across all comparable measures, with overall sentiment remaining strong and broadly consistent across UBS and former Credit Suisse employees. That sense of shared purpose has been a driving force behind our success. More importantly, it gives me confidence that we can continue to evolve as a firm and unlock the growth opportunities that lie ahead. Increasingly, technology and AI are amplifying the ability of our people to serve clients and operate as a more integrated firm. 
 Speaker 2 0:06:24 
 Our progress was recently validated by the 2026 Evident AI Index, with UBS recognized as the global leader in responsible AI and talent development in banking. Of course, another defining factor for the future of UBS is the ongoing parliamentary process related to banking regulation in Switzerland. I am convinced that, as was the case in March 2023, we are once again in a critical juncture where the course for the coming decades will be set for the Swiss Financial Center. September's outcome in the Upper House is very concerning. We have made every effort to engage and contribute constructively to create a basis for a truly democratic process. Our goal has been and remains to reach a solution that balances financial stability, taxpayer protection, and competitiveness. Unfortunately, the latest proposal on the table also fails to achieve that balance. 
 Speaker 2 0:07:43 
 It continues to disregard the serious concerns raised by the overwhelming majority of respondents to the consultation and would excessively tighten capital requirements that are already among the most stringent globally. Just as troubling is the failure to consider the consequences for our shareholders, who remain the first line of defense in periods of stress, and whose critical financial support during the acquisition helped protect Switzerland's reputation and financial stability. We will continue to engage constructively in the hope that the Parliament will reach a solution that supports the country financial stability without imposing undue cost on UBS's shareholders, clients, and employees, and without impacting its long-term competitive position. The ongoing debate is generating considerable attention, leading to a lot of speculation, opinions, and requests for clarification from all of our stakeholders. We do not intend to address everything, but on one topic, we want to be very clear. 
 Speaker 2 0:09:09 
 For UBS, the top priority is to protect the long-term interests of our shareholders, clients, and employees around the world. In a very competitive environment, it is essential to be able to continue to grow sustainably while remaining strategically committed to our diversified business model and our global and regional footprint, which allow us to create value for all of our stakeholders. After more than three years of disciplined execution, we are on track to complete the integration by year-end and have strong momentum across our businesses. With that, let me hand over to Todd. 
 Speaker 3 0:10:01 
 Thank you, Sergio, and good morning, everyone. In the third quarter, we delivered reported net profit of $2.7 billion and earnings per share of $0.85. On an underlying basis, our pre-tax profit was $4.1 billion, up 14%, with a return on CET1 capital of 16.7% and a cost-income ratio of 68.7%. Total revenues increased 10%, outpacing expense growth. Within our core franchises, excluding litigation, we delivered four points of positive operating leverage on 3% higher revenues and lower costs. Moving to slide six. This quarter's strong performance was underpinned by year-on-year profit growth in each of our businesses, alongside continued progress on the integration, now in its final stages. Reported results included integration costs of $452 million and a charge of $346 million from the repurchase of around $10 billion of high-cost Credit Suisse liabilities. 
 Speaker 3 0:11:10 
 The debt repurchase accelerates the reduction of the funding drag in Non-core and Legacy, while also supporting net interest income in GWM and P&C going forward. The effective tax rate in the quarter was 24.7%, slightly elevated as the legal provisions recorded in NCL are not expected to result in a tax benefit. Turning to our cost update on slide seven. With $13.2 billion of gross cost reductions already delivered, including $0.6 billion in the third quarter, we expect to deliver $0.5 billion more in the fourth quarter, bringing the total to around $13.7 billion, above our $13.5 billion ambition. Accelerated delivery of integration milestones has enabled us to identify additional synergies supporting this expected outperformance. Capturing these opportunities entails additional costs. 
 Speaker 3 0:12:13 
 As we complete the program at year-end, we expect around $0.5 billion of integration-related expenses in the fourth quarter, bringing the final cost to achieve multiple to around 1.1 times at historical FX rates, in line with guidance and a strong outcome given the integration scale and complexity. Total headcount at quarter end was 110,000, 2% lower sequentially and 30% below our 2022 baseline. Similarly, over the same period, we've reduced the group's operating expenses by almost 30% when excluding litigation, variable compensation, and currency effects. As the integration program concludes, our focus shifts from capturing related synergies to sustaining both a structurally efficient cost base and disciplined resource allocation. Together, these generate capacity for growth and attractive capital returns to shareholders. Turning to slide eight. As of the end of September, our balance sheet for All Seasons consisted of $1.7 trillion in total assets. 
 Speaker 3 0:13:30 
 Loan balances and deposits were down 1% sequentially, as positive net new lending and deposit flows across GWM and P&C were more than offset by FX translation. Credit-impaired exposures remained at 1%, while group credit loss expense was $114 million, corresponding to an annualized cost of risk of 7 basis points, unchanged from the prior quarter. Tangible book value per share increased slightly sequentially as profit in the quarter was largely offset by net charges in OCI and share repurchases. Overall, we continue to maintain a strong and resilient balance sheet with total loss-absorbing capacity of $187 billion, a net stable funding ratio of 115%, and an LCR of 179%. Turning to slide 9. Our CET1 capital ratio at the end of September was 14.7%, and our CET1 leverage ratio was 4.6%. 
 Speaker 3 0:14:40 
 Our common equity tier 1 capital increased by $0.7 billion in the quarter, as earnings generation was partly offset by dividend accruals, reserves for share award hedges, and currency effects. Risk-weighted assets and leverage exposure decreased sequentially by 8 billion and 59 billion, respectively, reflecting lower asset levels and FX translation. Looking ahead, we expect to end 2026 with a CET1 capital ratio at or very close to our target of around 14%, including a potential accrual for the initial portion of intended 2027 share buybacks. As Sergio mentioned, next quarter we will update our capital return ambitions for 2027 as part of our strategic update. UBS AG's stand-alone fully applied CET1 capital ratio at quarter end increased modestly to 14.5%, as 3Q earnings and the effect of lower RWA were largely offset by a dividend accrual of $1.8 billion. 
 Speaker 3 0:15:50 
 Turning to our business divisions and starting on slide 10 with Global Wealth Management. GWM delivered a pre-tax profit of $2 billion, up 11%. Excluding nearly $200 million of litigation-related releases that benefited the prior year quarter, pre-tax profit increased by 25%, with double-digit growth across all regions. Clients are increasingly turning to UBS for our advice and global capabilities and entrusting us with more of their wealth. Net new assets were $55 billion, representing a 4.5% growth rate and bringing year-to-date NNA to $128 billion. Momentum was broad-based across regions led by APAC and the Americas. Invested assets increased 1% sequentially as flow performance was offset by FX translation. At the same time, demand for our CIO-led solutions remained strong, driving $13 billion of net new fee-generating assets in the quarter, with momentum across our My Way discretionary mandates, U.S. advisory, and alternatives. 
 Speaker 3 0:17:00 
 Client activity also supported $6 billion of net new loans in the quarter, driven by securities-based lending. We attracted $2 billion of net new deposits with inflows into fixed-term instruments, more than offsetting outflows from current accounts. Moving to our regions. In the Americas, we continue to execute with discipline against our strategic priorities, delivering further improvements in profitability and growth. Pre-tax profit increased by 28%, with a profit margin of 16%, up more than 2 percentage points, supported by record revenues. During the quarter, we added $17 billion of net new assets, driven by strong same-store performance. Net new loans were $4 billion, reflecting investments to strengthen our banking capabilities and extending the region's run of positive quarterly lending growth. 
 Speaker 3 0:17:57 
 In Asia Pacific, we delivered pre-tax profit growth of 19% and a profit margin of 45%, while expanding our client advisor team and investing in capabilities across priority markets and client segments. Net new assets and net new fee-generating assets grew at annualized rates of 9% and 8%, respectively. Over 20 billion of NNFGA over the past 12 months drove a 20% increase in recurring revenues. These results demonstrate how deeper mandate penetration, stronger portfolio construction, and a broader offering are improving client outcomes and further strengthening the durability of our revenues across GWM, and particularly in Asia Pacific. Excluding litigation, EMEA increased pre-tax profit by 39%, benefiting from 13 percentage points of positive operating leverage and delivering a profit margin of 37%. 
 Speaker 3 0:18:56 
 The region also generated 9 billion of net new assets, reflecting solid underlying business momentum and the growing benefits of our fully integrated platform following the completion of the client account migration earlier this year. The benefits of the Swiss platform migration are particularly evident in our wealth franchise in Switzerland, where pre-tax profit excluding litigation increased 34%, reflecting broad-based growth across revenue lines and disciplined cost management. The Swiss team also maintained strong momentum in attracting client assets, generating 12 billion of NNA in the quarter, equivalent to 5% annualized growth. Turning to divisional revenues, which increased by 8%. Recurring net fee income grew by 9% to $3.8 billion on positive market performance and over 70 billion of net new fee-generating assets over the past 12 months. Transaction-based income increased by 4% to $1.3 billion, supported by demand for structured products and wealth planning. 
 Speaker 3 0:20:03 
 In the Americas, transactional revenues were 11% higher, reflecting strong client engagement and continued collaboration with the Investment Bank. While APAC delivered 2% growth against an exceptional prior year quarter. Net interest income of $1.8 billion rose 8% year-over-year and was modestly up over the prior quarter. Sequentially, higher deposit margins and loan volumes were broadly offset by current account shifts into fixed-term deposits. For the fourth quarter, we expect higher rates and lending growth to support a low single-digit sequential increase in GWM net interest income, also accounting for modest deposit mix effects. Operating expenses rose by 6%. When excluding variable compensation, litigation, and currency effects, costs declined by 4%. Turning to Personal & Corporate Banking on slide 11. P&C delivered its strongest quarter since the acquisition with pre-tax profit of CHF 813 million, up 22%, and an underlying pre-tax return on equity above 18%. 
 Speaker 3 0:21:14 
 With all clients now on a single platform and substantial progress in retiring legacy infrastructure, we're capturing meaningful cost efficiencies. The completion of client migrations earlier this year has also freed up capacity for P&C to deepen client relationships and capture market share. As a result, we saw strong momentum across the franchise. We attracted net new clients, grew both loans and deposits, and generated annualized net new investment product growth of 7%. This supported a 4% increase in revenues, while disciplined execution converted that momentum into 9 points of positive operating leverage. Despite the continued zero interest rate environment, net interest income was 2% higher year-on-year and 3% higher sequentially, driven by strong lending momentum. For the fourth quarter, we expect P&C net interest income in Swiss franc terms to increase slightly, supported by continued balance sheet growth. 
 Speaker 3 0:22:18 
 Non-interest revenues increased 5%, driven by personal banking, which benefited from higher custody, mandate, and card fees. In corporate and institutional clients, strength in payments and trade finance offset softer syndicated finance activity, although the pipeline remains strong. Net credit loss expense was CHF 27 million, as charges on non-performing loans were partly offset by model releases on the performing portfolio, reflecting the resilience of our Swiss corporate loan book amid macroeconomic uncertainty. For the fourth quarter, assuming the Swiss credit outlook remains constructive, we expect further model releases to partly offset seasonally higher stage 3 charges. Operating expenses declined 5%, driven by continued synergy realization. Turning to slide 12, Asset Management delivered pre-tax profit of CHF 300 million, up 6%, and a cost-income ratio of 62%, reflecting improved operating efficiency and continued growth in our priority initiatives. Excluding the O'Connor exit, total revenues and management fees were broadly stable. 
 Speaker 3 0:23:32 
 Net new money was negative CHF 5 billion, reflecting money market outflows and institutional portfolio rebalancing following the recent completion of our custody platform consolidation. This was partly offset by positive flows into ETFs, SMAs, and Unified Global Alternatives. Within UGA, we attracted a record CHF 12.5 billion of quarterly new commitments across GWM and Asset Management, bringing invested assets to CHF 371 billion and demonstrating the strength of our integrated distribution model. Operating expenses declined 14%, or 11% excluding O'Connor, reflecting continued benefits from our platform investments. We expect the exit to have a broadly similar impact on the 4Q revenue and cost comparison, with limited effects thereafter. Onto slide 13, the Investment Bank delivered pre-tax profit of CHF 854 million, up 9%, and a pre-tax return on equity of 18%, combining strong earnings growth with disciplined use of capital. 
 Speaker 3 0:24:42 
 Global banking revenues were CHF 670 million, down 21% against a record third quarter last year. Capital markets revenues declined 6%, outperforming the fee pool. A 44% increase in ECM was more than offset by lower LCM revenues, reflecting lower sponsor activity. The growth in ECM, spanning all regions, reflects continued momentum in one of our core strategic priorities and strengthens our broader equities franchise. Advisory revenues declined 44% from a record prior year quarter, also reflecting transaction timing. This came amid a fee pool that remains concentrated in mega-cap transactions, where balance sheet commitment plays a more prominent role. Looking ahead, client engagement and origination remain strong across advisory and capital markets, supporting a robust pipeline. Assuming constructive market conditions, we expect this to translate into sequential growth in global banking revenues in the fourth quarter. 
 Speaker 3 0:25:47 
 Global markets revenues rose 17% to a third-quarter record of CHF 2.5 billion, with 3Q highs across APAC, the Americas, and Switzerland, and led by broad-based strength in equities. Equities grew 22%, with strong performance across financing, cash, and derivatives, supported by higher client balances, market share gains, and healthy client activity. FRC was 1% higher, with growth in FX and credit, and a gain on a strategic investment partly offset by lower rates revenues. For the fourth quarter, we expect a more typical sequential seasonal moderation in transaction volumes. In addition, a strong prior year period, which included a gain on disposal, may weigh on the year-on-year comparison. Operating expenses increased by 5%, driven by higher non-personnel costs. On slide 14, Non-core and Legacy generated third quarter pre-tax profit of CHF 360 million. 
 Speaker 3 0:26:50 
 This largely reflected continued progress in addressing legacy cases, with net income from the settlement of certain legal matters more than offsetting $275 million of litigation charges. Operating expenses excluding litigation declined 69% to $91 million, bringing cumulative cost reductions against the 2022 baseline above 90%. Building on this progress, we now expect to exit the year with around $300 million of annualized operating expenses, excluding litigation, with further reductions thereafter. Risk-weighted assets declined 0.4 billion sequentially, driven by further reductions in the credit and macro portfolios. Both costs and RWA are already below our year-end ambitions. A brief word on group items on slide 15. The reported pre-tax loss of $740 million primarily reflects the liability management transaction discussed earlier and $265 million of own credit and hedging losses on accrual accounted positions, mainly due to the sharp rise in U.S. dollar interest rates. 
 Speaker 3 0:28:01 
 Excluding the temporary P&L volatility from these own credit and hedging positions, the underlying pre-tax loss was $138 million, largely related to DTA funding. To conclude, strong revenues and disciplined cost management drove a return on CET1 capital of 17% and a cost-income ratio of 70% over the first nine months, positioning us well to achieve our 2026 exit ambitions. As the integration concludes, we're focused on building on this progress, investing in our strongest growth opportunities, and sustaining earnings growth and attractive returns for our shareholders. With that, let's open for questions. 
 Speaker 0 0:28:49 
 We will now begin the Q&A session for analysts and investors. Participants are requested to use only handsets while asking a question. Anyone who has a question may press star and one at this time. The first question comes from the line of Antonio Reale from Bank of America. Please go ahead. 
 Speaker 4 0:29:10 
 Hi. Morning, everyone. It's Antonio from Bank of America. I have a couple of questions, if I may please. The first one is on your latest thoughts on the capital proposal that's being currently discussed by Parliament. Of course, I've heard Sergio's remarks. There was a WAK meeting yesterday and the day before. There seems to be a few scenarios on the table based on what we read on the press, at least. I think you've been very clear in your views on both 90% CET1 backing and the 50/50 option. Now, what would a 75% scenario mean for UBS? I guess the capital costs of higher requirements goes well beyond the mere billion-dollar charge, but I'm keen to hear your thoughts on this. 
 Speaker 4 0:29:50 
 Related to that, how do you view, and the board of UBS view, the cost of any contingency actions here versus the potential long-term implications that higher capital requirements may have on your ability to compete as a global business? That would be my first question. Then if I may, related to net new asset growth in the U.S., we have seen a positive surprise this quarter. What do you see as the key driver of U.S. growth now that you have a banking license and we are through what seems to be the worst part of FA departures from here? Thank you. 
 Speaker 3 0:30:36 
 Antonio, let me start with the second question. Look, we are continuing to see the benefits of our investments in the U.S. in advisors, our platform and capabilities, and the client experience as evidenced by, as I mentioned in my comments, strong same-store flows and improving advisor productivity, as well as continued accretion in our banking KPIs and normalized net recruiting metrics. Regarding the latter, as mentioned previously, there is a time lag in reported flows, headcount, and production from FA movement that could have an albeit tapering effect in our metrics. We see recruited joiners and announced leavers returning to more typical levels at UBS, including relative to the broader industry. All of these things are helping to drive the improved NNA that we saw this quarter and making the Americas a meaningful contributor to full year 2026 NNA for the division overall. 
 Speaker 2 0:31:52 
 On the capital proposal, I think that it is clear that the ongoing process now with the lower house is leading into a new round of coverage and speculations about potential other changes to the 90% proposal made in the Upper House. To be honest, I do not think that it is appropriate for us to go into discussing every single numbers that is thrown out. You make a reference to one of that number, and the one that we publicly, myself and our chairman, commented on was the 50/50 proposal. While being still a very expensive outcome considering our current capital position and the true lessons learned of what happened with Credit Suisse, we felt that a 50/50 proposal was balancing the needs of financial stability and reinforcing the current regulatory requirements while allowing us to preserve a competitive position going forward. 
 Speaker 2 0:33:13 
 I will not comment any further on any numbers, as I mentioned. In respect of contingency plan, listen, we are not going to engage into debating internally and externally about what to do until things are finally approved and actually determined. It is clear that there is no rush for us to act or to take actions that are not in the interest of shareholders and clients because it is going to take time to implement this new regulation. Of course, we are going to, and we will assess, and we are assessing what are the long-term consequences for our ability to compete out of Switzerland. Because it is very clear that for our clients, they do appreciate Swissness like we do. Like we believe we contribute to the Swiss system. A passport is not enough nowadays. 
 Speaker 2 0:34:20 
 People are expecting also quality of products, competitive pricing, and an ability to serve them globally as we do. Therefore, I think that it's premature for us to really think about the long-term consequences of what will happen. 
 Speaker 4 0:34:38 
 Thank you. 
 Speaker 0 0:34:44 
 The next question comes from Anke Reingen from RBC. Please go ahead. 
 Speaker 5 0:34:50 
 Yeah, thank you very much for taking my questions. The first is just on the costs. I just wondered if you can confirm, give us some indication about what to expect for Q4. I guess Q3 was being relatively strong. We should have a good cost control Q4. We have additional cost savings coming in, but also seasonality. So the -1%, is there anything you would highlight, we should be a bit more cautious on the Q4 trends? And then I just wondered in terms of client engagement. Obviously, the start of Q4 has been very different versus Q3. And I was wondering if you can talk a bit more about the client engagement you're seeing in your wealth management operation aside from the seasonality. Thank you very much. 
 Speaker 3 0:35:40 
 Hi, Anke. Thanks for the question. First on costs. I think you summarized actually the Q4 outlook pretty well. On the one hand, we will continue to see the benefits of the integration, just given the integration costs we have been incurring, and therefore the saves that will become evident through our OpEx as we have been demonstrating each quarter. We have always said that we will run through the tape on 2026 and continue to work until the very end. That is still the plan. So we should still see some of those efficiencies and synergies coming through in Q4. As you said as well, Q4 does have some seasonality aspects in them. The bank levy is one example, but also just often we see some uptick in costs sequentially. 
 Speaker 3 0:36:39 
 So nothing I would call out, but you would expect that those trends of continued cost efficiency offset perhaps by some uptick in seasonality will inform the performance in Q4 on costs. On clients, look, it is fair to say the Q4 market environment thus far for investors has been mixed. When you look at, say, rising correlations, things like rising correlations, deterioration in credit conditions, higher bond yields, and renewed inflation concerns to just take a few factors, they are leading to more defensive positioning among our clients. Geopolitical developments, including elections, are adding to this more measured sentiment. So we still see opportunities to help clients diversify, manage risk, and put money to work selectively, including a more attractive fixed income yields. So we will stay close to clients and capitalize on the opportunities that present themselves in this environment at present. 
 Speaker 5 0:37:56 
 Thank you. 
 Speaker 0 0:38:00 
 The next question comes from the line of Chris Hallam from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead. 
 Speaker 6 0:38:05 
 Good morning, everybody, and thank you for taking my questions. First, a quick one just on the U.S. When should we expect the National Bank charter to begin to translate into a broader U.S. product offering and perhaps sort of meaningful deposit growth? I think I've just sort of lost track on timings on that topic. Then second, to come back to the domicile point, there is an interesting tension within the group because, on the one hand, businesses such as the IB are relatively capital intensive, where the Swiss domicile may be less strategically important. While on the other hand, you've got more capital-light businesses such as GWM, which arguably derive significant value from that Swiss brand. 
 Speaker 6 0:38:46 
 How do you weigh those competing considerations and I guess also the strategic value of the interlinkages between those two distinct type of businesses when you're assessing whether Switzerland does remain the optimal domicile for the group, as you said earlier, from the perspective of shareholders, clients, and also other stakeholders? Thank you.
